## Archiving and registering a reanalysis {#every-reanalysis-leaves-a-public-trail .smaller}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
**OSF**, the Open Science Framework: a public repository in which data, code and **registrations** are timestamped and citable.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
A registration is a **frozen, dated snapshot of a plan**. Anyone can check what you said you would do, and when.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
You need no account today. We are going to *read* OSF the way that reviewers do.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
The robustness study itself was registered there: its scoring rules – same conclusion? effect size within ±0.05 *d*? – were filed **after the analysts had been recruited and before any analysis began**; 74% of the reanalyses reached the same conclusion, and 34% came within ±0.05 *d*.
:::
::::

::: {.src}
Preregistrations osf.io/4ev9t (pp. 2 and 9) and osf.io/y4evp; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness [p. 136].
:::

::: notes
Outside a classroom, an analysis plan is preregistered by filing it in a public registry. Everything with which you have worked in this workshop, the dataset, my analysis script and the codebook, is kept at a permanent public address on the Open Science Framework. [advance] The OSF does two jobs. It archives materials, which is the only reason why you could stand in the place of a real analyst at all, [advance] and it registers plans, a registration being a frozen, timestamped snapshot of what you intend to do, filed before you do it, which nobody, you included, can quietly edit afterwards. [advance] You need no account for any of this today, since we read the OSF as a reviewer or a sceptical reader would. [advance] The robustness study, in which you have worked as analyst no. 6, was itself registered there: its rules for judging the results, what counts as the same conclusion and how close counts as close for an effect size, were filed after the analysts had been recruited and before any of them had started. The seventy-four per cent that reached the same conclusion and the thirty-four per cent within five hundredths of a Cohen's d carry weight for that reason, since nobody could move the criteria once the results were in.
:::

## Three OSF addresses {#three-addresses-three-jobs}

::: {.urlbox}
[osf.io/8rtwe](https://osf.io/8rtwe) [– the archival record of the robustness study: analyst C6HJR, frozen as submitted]{.fs-80}
:::

::: {.urlbox .fragment}
[osf.io/6zqct](https://osf.io/6zqct) [– the maintained fork: the script, the codebook, the workshop's data]{.fs-80}
:::

::: {.urlbox .fragment}
[osf.io/h7432](https://osf.io/h7432) [– the full SCORE dossier on the paper: all the reports and their verdicts]{.fs-80}
:::

::: notes
Each of these addresses does a different job. The first is the official archive, the component of the robustness study for analyst C6HJR, frozen at the moment of submission and never touched again, which is what an archive is for and also its limit, since an archive cannot be updated as a project moves on. [advance] The second is the maintained fork, in which the working materials are updated and from which this workshop fetches its data, and a project that expects to keep changing usually needs both, an archive to preserve the record and a fork to keep the materials current. [advance] The third is the full SCORE dossier on this paper, with every report on the reproduction, the robustness study and the replication, all public, which the companion module on repositories reads as a record.
:::

## Preregistration templates {#two-templates-one-choice}

::: {.small}
- In your report: the **AsPredicted short form**, adapted for data you already hold – eight plain-language questions (on OSF: "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org")
- The fuller tool for our job: the **secondary-data template** (van den Akker et al. 2021, *Meta-Psychology*) – 25 questions, built for reanalysing data you already hold
- Both templates are in your reading
:::

::: notes
There are two templates, and the workshop uses one of them. The block in your report follows the short form of AsPredicted, eight questions in plain language, written for people who have not yet collected their data, so that its first question has, for us, the awkward answer that we already hold everything. The secondary-data template of van den Akker and colleagues, with twenty-five questions, was built for that situation, and our block borrows its section on what you already know about the data and calls it the data-in-hand statement.
:::

## The eight AsPredicted questions {#eight-questions-your-answers-already-mapped .smaller}

| AsPredicted asks | Your block answers |
|---|---|
| Q1 Have data been collected? | "It's complicated – I already hold them" + what I already know |
| Q2 Main question / hypothesis? | the claim, in your one sentence |
| Q3 Dependent variable? | your **frame set** and **scoring rule** |
| Q4 Conditions? | your options on the other decisions of the menu |
| Q5 Analyses? | your model + your support/undermine rule |
| Q6 Outliers / exclusions? | your **sample** decision |
| Q7 Sample size? | N = 270 country-years, fewer if your sample or series leaves some out |
| Q8 Anything else? | your DAG-grounded justification |

::: notes
Each question of AsPredicted maps onto a decision from an earlier task. The claim in the sentence that you wrote earlier answers question two, and your frame set and scoring rule make the dependent variable of question three. Your options on the other decisions of the menu are your conditions, your sample decision is the rule of exclusion, and the sample size is two hundred and seventy country-years, fewer if your sample or your published series leaves some out. Question one, which AsPredicted handles badly for us, you answer directly: the data exist, you hold them, and you say what you already know, including that the reproduced specification comes out at minus three point eight zero four.
:::
